title: St Lucy (13 December)
hook: in Sweden, girls in white with candle crowns bring light in the darkest weeks

segments.voice: Yesterday, St Nicholas: a bag of gold through a window at night, and no one told. Your line was give in secret.

It's still pitch black outside. In a Swedish house, a door opens and a girl walks in wearing a long white gown with a red sash, and on her head a crown of greenery with candles burning in it. She carries a tray of coffee and saffron buns, and she's singing. Across Sweden the same scene plays out that morning, in weeks when the northern sun barely shows. The girl is playing a part: a young woman from Sicily, a long way south.

Lucy lived in Syracuse, on the island of Sicily, when Christians there could be put to death for their faith. Tradition remembers her as a young woman who gave away what had been saved for her marriage to feed the poor, and who died a martyr rather than give up her faith. Beyond that, the stories grew in the telling. One told in the north says Lucy brought food to Christians hiding underground, and wore candles on her head so both hands were free to carry it. It's a story, not history, but it explains the crown. Why would Sweden, long shaped by the Lutheran church, keep an early martyr's day? Partly because of when it falls. Mid-December in the north is the deep end of the dark. A girl walking in with light on her head, in the blackest hour of the morning, says something without a word. John's Gospel says it in words: "And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not." Some readers hear understood in that word comprehended; others hear overcame, as if the darkness tried to grasp the light and put it out. Either way, the light is still shining. And Jesus hands that light to ordinary people in the Sermon on the Mount: "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven." That's this week's saints: real people who carried a little light into a dark place.

Stand a moment in a dim room, then bring in one small light, a candle if it's safe, a lamp, or your phone screen turned low, and set it in the middle. Notice how far one small light reaches. If you pray, you can say the words from John, the light shineth in darkness; if you don't, just watch the light and let it be enough.
St Lucy. A young martyr of Syracuse, remembered for feeding the poor, and in Sweden by girls in white with a crown of candles in the dark of December.
Your line: light in the dark. A week of saints and candles, from Polycarp to Lucy. Day one thousand eight.

howItsDone: In Sweden and other Nordic countries, Lucia processions are held in homes, schools and churches, led by a girl in white with a crown of candles; Catholic and Orthodox churches also keep her day as a martyr's feast.

fork.setup: you're Lucy, a young Christian in Syracuse. money has been set aside for your marriage. what do you do with it?
options: keep it safe for the wedding.
give it away to feed the poor.
hide it until the persecution is over.
fork.reveal: tradition remembers her giving it to the poor — and that is part of why she is honored as a saint.

chat.says: Why do girls here wear candle crowns for a saint from Sicily?
options: St Lucy's day falls in the deep northern dark; tradition says she fed the poor.
Lucy was a Swedish princess who lit candles for the king every winter.
Lucy sailed north to Sweden with candles to preach in the winter dark.
chat.meaning: Lucy's day falls in mid-December, the deep end of the northern dark. Tradition remembers her feeding the poor; a story says candles freed her hands.

Syracuse.meaning: an ancient city on Sicily, Lucy's home

martyr.meaning: someone who dies rather than give up their faith
